---
title: "Processes and Threads — Who Owns Memory?"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

Imagine two chefs working in two different kitchens. Each kitchen is a process with its own address space; chefs sharing one kitchen are threads. They can share ingredients, but must coordinate access.

## The core concept

A process provides a resource and protection boundary; a thread is an execution path within a process. Neither is exactly one CPU core.

## Express it mathematically

$$
P=\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** P denotes one process in this teaching abstraction, and T_i are its n threads; the braces indicate a set. This is a conceptual relationship, not a full kernel implementation definition.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For n=2, P contains T_1 and T_2. If both increment one shared counter from 0 without synchronisation, a lost update may leave 1 instead of 2. If they hold a lock across the read-modify-write, the counter reaches 2.

## Why it works

Threads in the same process generally share a virtual address space; processes normally have distinct virtual address spaces, though OS facilities explicitly allow shared memory. Scheduling concerns execution units, while memory isolation concerns address-space mappings.

## Go one level deeper

A process can have one thread or many; a thread may block or be runnable. Linux represents schedulable execution units as tasks and uses sharing flags to express common resources.

## Common misunderstanding

Do not conclude that two threads always run in parallel. On one core they may interleave; on multiple cores they may actually overlap.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
